targets.name: Sum, product and quotient rules
targets.idea: (a) follows from the sum rule for limits (4.4). For (b) split the increment of the product as $f(t)g(t)-f(x)g(x)=f(t)\,[g(t)-g(x)]+g(x)\,[f(t)-f(x)]$, divide by $t-x$, and use $f(t)\to f(x)$, which is Theorem 5.2. For (c) put the increment of $f/g$ over the common denominator $g(t)g(x)$; by 5.2 again it tends to $g(x)^2\neq0$.

targets.name: Chain rule
targets.statement:
Let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at a point $x\in[a,b]$; let $g$ be defined on an interval $I$ containing the range of $f$ and differentiable at the point $f(x)$. Then $h(t)=g(f(t))$ $(a\le t\le b)$ is differentiable at $x$, and
$$h'(x)=g'(f(x))\,f'(x).$$
targets.idea: Dividing by $f(t)-f(x)$ is not allowed, since it may vanish for $t$ near $x$. Instead encode both derivatives with error terms: $f(t)-f(x)=(t-x)\,[f'(x)+u(t)]$ and $g(s)-g(y)=(s-y)\,[g'(y)+v(s)]$ with $y=f(x)$ and $u(t)\to0$, $v(s)\to0$. Substituting $s=f(t)$ gives $h(t)-h(x)=(t-x)\,[f'(x)+u(t)]\,[g'(y)+v(f(t))]$; continuity of $f$ makes $v(f(t))\to0$ (4.7), and the limit rules (4.4) finish.

targets.name: Interior extrema have zero derivative
targets.statement: Let $f$ be defined on $[a,b]$. If $f$ has a local maximum at a point $x\in(a,b)$ and $f'(x)$ exists, then $f'(x)=0$. The same conclusion holds at a local minimum.
targets.idea: Choose $\delta$ as in Definition 5.7 with $a<x-\delta<x+\delta<b$. For $x-\delta<t<x$ the quotient $\frac{f(t)-f(x)}{t-x}$ has a numerator $\le0$ and a negative denominator, so it is $\ge0$; for $x<t<x+\delta$ it is $\le0$. Letting $t\to x$ from the left and from the right gives $f'(x)\ge0$ and $f'(x)\le0$.

targets.name: Linearity, order, additivity and bounds
targets.statement:
(a) If $f_1,f_2\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$ on $[a,b]$, then $f_1+f_2\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$ and $cf\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$ for every constant $c$ and $f\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$, with $\int(f_1+f_2)\,d\alpha=\int f_1\,d\alpha+\int f_2\,d\alpha$ and $\int cf\,d\alpha=c\int f\,d\alpha$.
(b) If moreover $f_1\le f_2$ on $[a,b]$, then $\int f_1\,d\alpha\le\int f_2\,d\alpha$.
(c) If $f\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$ on $[a,b]$ and $a<c<b$, then $f\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$ on $[a,c]$ and on $[c,b]$, and $\int_a^c f\,d\alpha+\int_c^b f\,d\alpha=\int_a^b f\,d\alpha$.
(d) If $f\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$ and $|f|\le M$ on $[a,b]$, then $\bigl|\int_a^b f\,d\alpha\bigr|\le M[\alpha(b)-\alpha(a)]$.
(e) If $f\in\mathscr R(\alpha_1)$ and $f\in\mathscr R(\alpha_2)$, then $f\in\mathscr R(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)$ and $\int f\,d(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)=\int f\,d\alpha_1+\int f\,d\alpha_2$; if $c>0$ is constant, $f\in\mathscr R(c\alpha)$ and $\int f\,d(c\alpha)=c\int f\,d\alpha$.
targets.idea: Each part comes from an inequality for sums. For (a): on every cell $\sup(f_1+f_2)\le\sup f_1+\sup f_2$ and similarly for infima, so $L(P,f_1)+L(P,f_2)\le L(P,f)\le U(P,f)\le U(P,f_1)+U(P,f_2)$; choosing $P$ by 6.6 for both $f_1,f_2$ squeezes everything. (c) follows by always including $c$ in the partition, (b) and (d) by comparing sums term by term, and (e) because $\Delta(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)_i=\Delta\alpha_{1,i}+\Delta\alpha_{2,i}$.

targets.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
targets.statement:
If $f\in\mathscr R$ on $[a,b]$ and there is a differentiable function $F$ on $[a,b]$ with $F'=f$, then
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).$$
targets.idea: Given $\eps>0$ take $P$ with $U(P,f)-L(P,f)<\eps$. The mean value theorem gives $t_i\in(x_{i-1},x_i)$ with $F(x_i)-F(x_{i-1})=f(t_i)\Delta x_i$, so the tagged sum $\sum f(t_i)\Delta x_i$ telescopes to exactly $F(b)-F(a)$. By 6.7(c) it is also within $\eps$ of $\int_a^b f$. Note that $f$ need not be continuous — only integrable.

targets.name: Uniform convergence and integration
targets.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be monotonically increasing on $[a,b]$. Suppose $f_n\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$ on $[a,b]$ for $n=1,2,3,\dots$, and $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$. Then $f\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$ on $[a,b]$, and
$$\int_a^b f\,d\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n\,d\alpha$$
(in particular, the limit on the right exists).
targets.idea: Let $\eps_n=\sup_{[a,b]}|f_n-f|$. Then $f_n-\eps_n\le f\le f_n+\eps_n$, so the upper and lower integrals of $f$ lie between $\int(f_n-\eps_n)\,d\alpha$ and $\int(f_n+\eps_n)\,d\alpha$ and differ by at most $2\eps_n[\alpha(b)-\alpha(a)]$. Since $\eps_n\to0$ (7.9), $f\in\mathscr R(\alpha)$, and the same sandwich gives $\bigl|\int f\,d\alpha-\int f_n\,d\alpha\bigr|\le\eps_n[\alpha(b)-\alpha(a)]\to0$.

targets.name: Linear equations and integrating factors
targets.statement:
Let $a, b$ be continuous on an interval $I\ni t_0$. The linear equation $\dot x + a(t)\,x = b(t)$ has, for each $x_0$, exactly one solution on all of $I$ with $x(t_0) = x_0$, namely
$$x(t) = e^{-A(t)}\Big(x_0 + \int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(s)}\,b(s)\,ds\Big),\qquad A(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} a(s)\,ds.$$
It is the sum of the solution $x_0e^{-A(t)}$ of the homogeneous equation and the particular solution $x_p$ with $x_p(t_0) = 0$. The difference of any two solutions solves the homogeneous equation, so if $a(t)\ge\alpha>0$ all solutions approach one another like $e^{-\alpha (t-t_0)}$.
targets.idea: Multiplying by the *integrating factor* $\mu(t) = e^{A(t)}$ turns the left side into an exact derivative: $\mu(\dot x + a x) = (\mu x)'$, because $\dot\mu = a\mu$. So $(\mu x)' = \mu b$, and integrating from $t_0$ (pma-6.21) gives the formula; conversely the formula solves the equation by direct differentiation, and the same computation shows any solution must equal it. Linearity is what makes this possible: in $y = \mu x$ the equation no longer involves $y$ on the right, so solutions differ only by constants $y$-wise, i.e. by multiples of $e^{-A}$ in $x$. Solutions never blow up, since the formula is finite on all of $I$.

targets.name: Linear systems of ODEs
targets.statement: A *linear system* is an equation $\dot x=A(t)x+g(t)$ for $x(t)\in\R^n$, with $A$ an $n\times n$ matrix function and $g$ a vector function, both continuous. It is *homogeneous* when $g\equiv0$ and *autonomous* (constant coefficients) when $A$ does not depend on $t$. For the homogeneous system the map $x_0\mapsto x(t)$ is linear in the initial value: if $\varphi,\psi$ are solutions and $\alpha,\beta\in\R$, then $\alpha\varphi+\beta\psi$ is a solution (superposition), so the solutions form a vector space. The right-hand side is globally Lipschitz in $x$ on every bounded time interval, so solutions exist and are unique for all time.
targets.idea: Differentiation and matrix multiplication are linear, so $\frac{d}{dt}(\alpha\varphi+\beta\psi)=\alpha A\varphi+\beta A\psi=A(\alpha\varphi+\beta\psi)$. Since $|A(t)x-A(t)y|\le\|A(t)\|\,|x-y|$ the field is Lipschitz with constant $\max\|A\|$ on any compact time interval; Picard–Lindelöf (2.4) gives uniqueness and the linear growth bound $|f|\le\|A\||x|$ rules out blow-up, so solutions are global (this is the content of 2.12). Everything later in the chapter exploits the vector-space structure.

targets.name: e^{tA} is the flow of ẋ = Ax
targets.statement:
For a constant matrix $A$ the unique solution of $\dot x=Ax$, $x(0)=x_0$ is $x(t)=e^{tA}x_0$, defined for all $t\in\R$. Consequently the flow $\Phi_t=e^{tA}$ is a group of invertible linear maps ($\Phi_{s+t}=\Phi_s\Phi_t$, $\Phi_0=I$) and
$$\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A,\qquad \det e^{tA}=e^{t\operatorname{tr}A}.$$
The columns of $e^{tA}$ are the solutions starting at the standard basis vectors, so $e^{tA}$ is a fundamental matrix with value $I$ at $t=0$.
targets.idea: Differentiating the series for $e^{tA}$ termwise (legitimate by the uniform convergence from 3.2) gives $Ae^{tA}$, and $e^{0}=I$, so $t\mapsto e^{tA}x_0$ solves the initial value problem. Uniqueness comes from Picard–Lindelöf (2.4) because the field is globally Lipschitz. The group law is then uniqueness again: $t\mapsto e^{(s+t)A}x_0$ and $t\mapsto e^{tA}e^{sA}x_0$ solve the same problem. The determinant formula is Liouville's formula (3.11) at constant $A$.

targets.name: Change-of-basis formula
targets.statement:
Suppose $T\in\mathcal L(V)$ and $u_1,\dots,u_n$ and $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are bases of $V$. Let
$$A=\mathcal M\big(T,(u_1,\dots,u_n)\big),\quad B=\mathcal M\big(T,(v_1,\dots,v_n)\big),\quad C=\mathcal M\big(I,(u_1,\dots,u_n),(v_1,\dots,v_n)\big).$$
Then $A=C^{-1}BC$.
targets.idea: Write $T=I\,T\,I$ and apply 3.81 twice, routing through the basis $v$: $\mathcal M(T,(u))=\mathcal M(I,(v),(u))\,\mathcal M(T,(v))\,\mathcal M(I,(u),(v))$. The outer factors are $C^{-1}$ and $C$ by 3.82. In words: convert $u$-coordinates to $v$-coordinates, apply $T$ there, convert back.

targets.name: Minimizing distance to a subspace
targets.statement: Suppose $U$ is a finite-dimensional subspace of $V$, $v\in V$ and $u\in U$. Then $$\|v-P_Uv\|\le\|v-u\|,$$ with equality if and only if $u=P_Uv$. In words: $P_Uv$ is the unique point of $U$ closest to $v$.
targets.idea: Write $v-u=(v-P_Uv)+(P_Uv-u)$. The first piece lies in $U^\perp$ by 6.57(f) and the second lies in $U$, so Pythagoras (6.12) gives $$\|v-u\|^2=\|v-P_Uv\|^2+\|P_Uv-u\|^2\ge\|v-P_Uv\|^2,$$ with equality exactly when $P_Uv-u=0$. Combined with the formula 6.57(i) this solves concrete approximation problems: projecting $\sin x$ onto the polynomials of degree at most $5$ in $C[-\pi,\pi]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}fg$ gives $0.987862x-0.155271x^3+0.00564312x^5$, far better on $[-\pi,\pi]$ than the Taylor polynomial.

targets.name: Positive definite matrix
targets.statement:
A matrix $B \in \mathbf F^{n,n}$ is called **positive definite** if $B^* = B$ and
$$\langle Bx, x\rangle > 0 \quad\text{for every nonzero } x \in \mathbf F^n,$$
where $\mathbf F^n$ carries the Euclidean inner product and $x$ is viewed as a column. By 7.61, these are exactly the matrices of the positive invertible operators on $\mathbf F^n$.
targets.idea: This is 7.61 transferred to matrices: $B^* = B$ says the operator $x \mapsto Bx$ is self-adjoint (7.9), and the strict inequality then says it is positive and invertible. For a real symmetric $2$-by-$2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{bmatrix}$ the condition is $a > 0$ and $ac - b^2 > 0$ (both eigenvalues positive), and the curve $\langle Bx, x\rangle = 1$ is then an ellipse whose semi-axes point along the eigenvectors with lengths $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$.

targets.name: Linearity and monotonicity of expectation
targets.idea: Expectation is an integral, so (a)–(c) restate Lemma 1.4.5 (nonnegative case) and Theorem 1.4.7 (integrable case), together with $E(b)=b\,P(\Omega)=b$. Nothing about the joint behaviour of $X$ and $Y$ enters. Linearity holds however strongly the two variables depend on each other, even though the **spread** of $aX+bY$ depends on that dependence.

targets.name: Moments and variance
targets.statement:
For a positive integer $k$, $EX^k$ is the **$k$th moment** of $X$; the first moment $EX$ is the mean $\mu$. If $EX^2<\infty$, the **variance** is
$$\operatorname{var}(X)=E(X-\mu)^2=EX^2-\mu^2,$$
so $\operatorname{var}(X)\le EX^2$, and $\operatorname{var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{var}(X)$. By the change of variables formula all of these are integrals against the law of $X$: $EX^k=\int x^k\,\mu(dx)$. If $E|X|^k<\infty$ then $E|X|^j<\infty$ for $0<j<k$ (Exercise 1.6.11).
targets.idea: Expanding the square and using linearity: $E(X-\mu)^2=EX^2-2\mu EX+\mu^2=EX^2-\mu^2$. A moment exists only if the tail of the law decays fast enough: $E|X|^s<\infty$ asks that $\int s\,x^{s-1}P(|X|>x)\,dx$ converge (Lemma 2.2.13). Conversely, the full sequence of moments need not determine the law: Heyde's lognormal family is the classical example (Section 3.3.5).

targets.name: Strong law of large numbers (Etemadi)
targets.statement:
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be **pairwise independent** and identically distributed with $E|X_i|<\infty$. Let $\mu=EX_i$ and $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$. Then
$$\frac{S_n}{n}\to\mu\quad\text{almost surely.}$$
targets.idea: Treat $X^+$ and $X^-$ separately, so assume $X_i\ge0$. Truncate: $Y_k=X_k1(|X_k|\le k)$; by Lemma 2.4.2 it suffices to show $T_n/n\to\mu$ for $T_n=Y_1+\dots+Y_n$. Pairwise independence is enough for variances to add, and Lemma 2.4.3 bounds $\sum_k\operatorname{var}(Y_k)/k^2\le4E|X_1|$. Along the geometric times $k(n)=[\alpha^n]$ Chebyshev and Borel–Cantelli (2.3.1) give $T_{k(n)}/k(n)\to\mu$; since $T_m$ is increasing, for $k(n)\le m<k(n+1)$ the ratio is trapped between $\mu/\alpha$ and $\alpha\mu$ asymptotically. Let $\alpha\downarrow1$.

fields.label: statement-scope
fields.text: What the body does to a drug can be sorted into four processes. Absorption moves the drug from its site of administration into the blood (an intravenous dose skips it). Distribution carries it from the blood into tissues and back. Metabolism, mostly in the liver, chemically alters it, and excretion, mostly by the kidneys, removes it unchanged or as metabolites. The last two together are elimination. For an oral dose the blood leaving the gut passes through the liver first, so some drug can be metabolized before it ever reaches the general circulation (the first-pass effect, 1.6). At every instant the amounts in all places add up to the dose that was given.A deliberately simple linear model: first-order flows, the whole oral dose absorbed, instant mixing inside plasma and inside tissue. Real drugs have several tissues, active transport, saturable steps and incomplete absorption.

fields.label: proof
fields.text: ADME is bookkeeping. Each process is a flow between two places, and in the simplest models the flow is proportional to the amount in the source (a rate constant times an amount). Writing the flows down gives a small system of linear differential equations in which the total amount is conserved, so the stacked picture of "where is the drug" always sums to the dose; only the split changes. Fast absorption empties the gut early; strong tissue uptake parks drug away from the blood; high hepatic or renal function pushes drug into the "gone" columns sooner.The sum rule for derivatives (pma 5.3) turns the five displayed model balances into a conservation check. In G+P+T+M+UG+P+T+M+UG+P+T+M+U, each gut-to-plasma, plasma-to-tissue, return, metabolism and excretion flow occurs once with each sign, so the derivative of the total is zero. Its initial value is the administered dose. M and U are cumulative parent-dose equivalents in this bookkeeping model; this cancellation is not a claim that every real metabolite has the same molecular mass as its parent.

fields.text: If absorption and elimination are first-order (the system is linear and time-invariant), the concentration after repeated doses DDD given at times 0,τ,2τ,…0,\tau,2\tau,\dots0,τ,2τ,… is the sum of the single-dose curves, each shifted to its dose time: C(t)=∑n≥0,  nτ≤tC1(t−nτ)C(t)=\sum_{n\ge 0,\; n\tau\le t} C_1(t-n\tau)C(t)=∑n≥0,nτ≤t​C1​(t−nτ). The sum climbs in a sawtooth and, when k>0k>0k>0, approaches a repeating pattern.Holds only for linear kinetics: first-order absorption and elimination, constant parameters. fields.label: proof
fields.text: Linearity means the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the responses, so a second dose does not care that a first one is still in the body: each dose decays on its own schedule (the one-compartment decay of pharm-2.1). Adding the shifted copies gives the whole history. Nothing here needs a differential equation per dose; the same sum is recovered by integrating the ODE across the dose jumps, which the readout does as a check.The superposition argument is the linear-solution property in ode 3.1 applied between the prescribed dose jumps. Each shifted single-dose state solves the same homogeneous disposition system after its own arrival; differentiation of their finite sum gives that system between doses, while the sum has exactly the required bolus increments. For an oral dose include the linear gut compartment as part of the state. Uniqueness on each interval then identifies this sum with the piecewise initial-value solution. fields.label: statement-scope
fields.text: With linear kinetics and equal doses DDD (bioavailable fraction FFF) every τ\tauτ, the average concentration over a dosing interval at steady state is Cˉss=1τ∫0τCss(t) dt=F DCL τ\bar C_{ss}=\dfrac{1}{\tau}\int_0^\tau C_{ss}(t)\,dt=\dfrac{F\,D}{\mathrm{CL}\,\tau}Cˉss​=τ1​∫0τ​Css​(t)dt=CLτFD​: dosing rate divided by clearance. It does not depend on the volume of distribution or on the absorption rate.Linear, time-invariant kinetics. With saturable elimination or changing clearance the average is not given by this formula (chapter 5).

fields.label: proof
fields.text: The area under one single-dose curve is FD/CLF D/\mathrm{CL}FD/CL (pharm-1.5). At steady state the superposed tails of all earlier doses fill each interval, and the area per interval equals the area of one complete dose curve (the part of its tail falling into later intervals is exactly compensated by the earlier tails entering this one). Dividing the area FD/CLFD/\mathrm{CL}FD/CL by τ\tauτ gives the mean. Absorption speed reshapes the curve but cannot change its area.Passing from finitely many previous doses to the periodic profile needs a justified limit under the integral. For these positive-rate one-compartment IV or Bateman responses, the old-dose tails on one dosing interval are bounded by a summable geometric sequence (with an additional linear age factor in the equal-rate Bateman case). The partial sums therefore converge uniformly on that interval. fields.text: What the body does to a drug can be sorted into four processes. Absorption moves the drug from its site of administration into the blood (an intravenous dose skips it). Distribution carries it from the blood into tissues and back. Metabolism, mostly in the liver, chemically alters it, and excretion, mostly by the kidneys, removes it unchanged or as metabolites. The last two together are elimination. For an oral dose the blood leaving the gut passes through the liver first, so some drug can be metabolized before it ever reaches the general circulation (the first-pass effect, 1.6). At every instant the amounts in all places add up to the dose that was given.A deliberately simple linear model: first-order flows, the whole oral dose absorbed, instant mixing inside plasma and inside tissue. M and U are cumulative parent-dose equivalents in this bookkeeping model; this cancellation is not a claim that every real metabolite has the same molecular mass as its parent.

Fractions use one dose before 30 minutes and two after a second bolus.

fields.text: If absorption and elimination are first-order (the system is linear and time-invariant), the concentration after repeated doses DDD given at times 0,τ,2τ,…0,\tau,2\tau,\dots0,τ,2τ,… is the sum of the single-dose curves, each shifted to its dose time: C(t)=∑n≥0,  nτ≤tC1(t−nτ)C(t)=\sum_{n\ge 0,\; n\tau\le t} C_1(t-n\tau)C(t)=∑n≥0,nτ≤t​C1​(t−nτ). The sum climbs in a sawtooth and, when k>0k>0k>0, approaches a repeating pattern.Holds only for linear kinetics: first-order absorption and elimination, constant parameters. It fails for saturable elimination (chapter 5), time-varying clearance, or autoinduction. Values here are a model (V = 40 L, dose 100 mg), not a particular drug.

fields.label: proof
fields.text: Linearity means the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the responses, so a second dose does not care that a first one is still in the body: each dose decays on its own schedule (the one-compartment decay of pharm-2.1). Adding the shifted copies gives the whole history. Nothing here needs a differential equation per dose; the same sum is recovered by integrating the ODE across the dose jumps, which the readout does as a check.The superposition argument is the linear-solution property in ode 3.1 applied between the prescribed dose jumps. Each shifted single-dose state solves the same homogeneous disposition system after its own arrival; differentiation of their finite sum gives that system between doses, while the sum has exactly the required bolus increments. For an oral dose include the linear gut compartment as part of the state. Uniqueness on each interval then identifies this sum with the piecewise initial-value solution. Saturable loss or coefficients that change with dose break this argument.

With saturable elimination or changing clearance the average is not given by this formula (chapter 5).

fields.label: proof
fields.text: The area under one single-dose curve is FD/CLF D/\mathrm{CL}FD/CL (pharm-1.5). At steady state the superposed tails of all earlier doses fill each interval, and the area per interval equals the area of one complete dose curve (the part of its tail falling into later intervals is exactly compensated by the earlier tails entering this one). Dividing the area FD/CLFD/\mathrm{CL}FD/CL by τ\tauτ gives the mean. Absorption speed reshapes the curve but cannot change its area.Passing from finitely many previous doses to the periodic profile needs a justified limit under the integral. For these positive-rate one-compartment IV or Bateman responses, the old-dose tails on one dosing interval are bounded by a summable geometric sequence (with an additional linear age factor in the equal-rate Bateman case). The partial sums therefore converge uniformly on that interval. Uniform convergence and integration, pma 7.16, let their integrals tend to the integral of the periodic profile; partitioning the single-dose time axis into consecutive intervals gives the full single-dose AUC. This is a steady-state limit, not the area during a finite startup interval.

This mathematical smoothing does not guarantee efficacy or safety after a miss.Model: independent misses, no “catching up”, a fixed dose time each day, oral absorption ka=1.5k_a=1.5ka​=1.5 h−1^{-1}−1, history of perfect adherence before day 0. The window is illustrative, not drug-specific.

fields.label: proof
fields.text: The concentration is the superposition of the doses actually taken (pharm-4.1): each missed dose deletes one term. The missing single-dose contribution has a decaying tail; one elimination half-life halves its terminal component rather than ending its effect. The relevant comparison is this decay time against the dosing interval. With a long half-life the missing term is small relative to the stored sum from many earlier doses; with a short one it is most of the signal.Write the taken-dose indicators as independent Bernoulli variables B_j with mean a. Linearity of expectation (prob 1.6.1) gives expected input aNDaNDaND over N planned doses and, in a stationary dosing history, expected concentration equal to a times the perfect-adherence periodic curve. The strong law prob 2.4.1 applies because these indicators are identically distributed, pairwise independent and bounded: their realized average tends to a almost surely. Integrated mass balance over N intervals then gives the same long-run time-mean concentration, since the remaining gut/body amount is bounded for fixed positive rates and contributes a vanishing endpoint term after division by N. This is an asymptotic model result; the finite 14-day history with a perfect-adherence lead-in and the 60-member sampled band statistic are not exact realizations of that mean.

fields.text: After an intravenous bolus into a two-compartment body the plasma curve has two phases. In the early distribution (α\alphaα) phase the concentrations in the two compartments differ, and both redistribution and elimination lower the central concentration. When the fast mode has died out the concentration ratio C2/C1C_2/C_1C2​/C1​ has become constant and the body behaves as one pool: the elimination (β\betaβ) phase, in which both compartments decline together at rate β\betaβ and the loss is by clearance. The peripheral amount is greatest exactly when C1=C2C_1=C_2C1​=C2​.Two linear compartments with elimination from the central one. The 5 % criterion for the end of the distribution phase is a convention chosen here; there is no sharp boundary.

fields.label: statement-scope
fields.text: What the body does to a drug can be sorted into four processes. Absorption moves the drug from its site of administration into the blood (an intravenous dose skips it). Distribution carries it from the blood into tissues and back. Metabolism, mostly in the liver, chemically alters it, and excretion, mostly by the kidneys, removes it unchanged or as metabolites. The last two together are elimination. For an oral dose the blood leaving the gut passes through the liver first, so some drug can be metabolized before it ever reaches the general circulation (the first-pass effect, 1.6). At every instant the amounts in all places add up to the dose that was given.Holds when A deliberately simple linear model: first-order flows, the whole oral dose absorbed, instant mixing inside plasma and inside tissue. Real drugs have several tissues, active transport, saturable steps and incomplete absorption.

fields.label: proof
fields.text: ADME is bookkeeping. Each process is a flow between two places, and in the simplest models the flow is proportional to the amount in the source (a rate constant times an amount). Writing the flows down gives a small system of linear differential equations in which the total amount is conserved, so the stacked picture of "where is the drug" always sums to the dose; only the split changes. Fast absorption empties the gut early; strong tissue uptake parks drug away from the blood; high hepatic or renal function pushes drug into the "gone" columns sooner.The sum rule for derivatives (pma 5.3) turns the five displayed model balances into a conservation check. In G+P+T+M+UG+P+T+M+UG+P+T+M+U, each gut-to-plasma, plasma-to-tissue, return, metabolism and excretion flow occurs once with each sign, so the derivative of the total is zero. Its initial value is the administered dose. M and U are cumulative parent-dose equivalents in this bookkeeping model; this cancellation is not a claim that every real metabolite has the same molecular mass as its parent.

fields.text: Linearity means the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the responses, so a second dose does not care that a first one is still in the body: each dose decays on its own schedule (the one-compartment decay of pharm-2.1). Nothing here needs a differential equation per dose; the same sum is recovered by integrating the ODE across the dose jumps, which the readout does as a check.The superposition argument is the linear-solution property in ode 3.1 applied between the prescribed dose jumps. Each shifted single-dose state solves the same homogeneous disposition system after its own arrival; differentiation of their finite sum gives that system between doses, while the sum has exactly the required bolus increments. For an oral dose include the linear gut compartment as part of the state. Uniqueness on each interval then identifies this sum with the piecewise initial-value solution. Saturable loss or coefficients that change with dose break this argument.

fields.label: statement-scope
fields.text: What the body does to a drug can be sorted into four processes. Absorption moves the drug from its site of administration into the blood (an intravenous dose skips it). Distribution carries it from the blood into tissues and back. Metabolism, mostly in the liver, chemically alters it, and excretion, mostly by the kidneys, removes it unchanged or as metabolites. The last two together are elimination. For an oral dose the blood leaving the gut passes through the liver first, so some drug can be metabolized before it ever reaches the general circulation (the first-pass effect, 1.6). At every instant the amounts in all places add up to the dose that was given.Holds when A deliberately simple linear model: first-order flows, the whole oral dose absorbed, instant mixing inside plasma and inside tissue. Real drugs have several tissues, active transport, saturable steps and incomplete absorption.

fields.text: ADME is bookkeeping. Each process is a flow between two places, and in the simplest models the flow is proportional to the amount in the source (a rate constant times an amount). Writing the flows down gives a small system of linear differential equations in which the total amount is conserved, so the stacked picture of "where is the drug" always sums to the dose; only the split changes. Fast absorption empties the gut early; strong tissue uptake parks drug away from the blood; high hepatic or renal function pushes drug into the "gone" columns sooner.The sum rule for derivatives (pma 5.3) turns the five displayed model balances into a conservation check. In G+P+T+M+UG+P+T+M+UG+P+T+M+U, each gut-to-plasma, plasma-to-tissue, return, metabolism and excretion flow occurs once with each sign, so the derivative of the total is zero. Its initial value is the administered dose. M and U are cumulative parent-dose equivalents in this bookkeeping model; this cancellation is not a claim that every real metabolite has the same molecular mass as its parent.

fields.text: If absorption and elimination are first-order (the system is linear and time-invariant), the concentration after repeated doses DDD given at times 0,τ,2τ,…0,\tau,2\tau,\dots0,τ,2τ,… is the sum of the single-dose curves, each shifted to its dose time: C(t)=∑n≥0,  nτ≤tC1(t−nτ)C(t)=\sum_{n\ge 0,\; n\tau\le t} C_1(t-n\tau)C(t)=∑n≥0,nτ≤t​C1​(t−nτ). fields.text: Linearity means the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the responses, so a second dose does not care that a first one is still in the body: each dose decays on its own schedule (the one-compartment decay of pharm-2.1). Nothing here needs a differential equation per dose; the same sum is recovered by integrating the ODE across the dose jumps, which the readout does as a check.The superposition argument is the linear-solution property in ode 3.1 applied between the prescribed dose jumps. Each shifted single-dose state solves the same homogeneous disposition system after its own arrival; differentiation of their finite sum gives that system between doses, while the sum has exactly the required bolus increments. For an oral dose include the linear gut compartment as part of the state. Uniqueness on each interval then identifies this sum with the piecewise initial-value solution. fields.label: proof
fields.text: The area under one single-dose curve is FD/CLF D/\mathrm{CL}FD/CL (pharm-1.5). At steady state the superposed tails of all earlier doses fill each interval, and the area per interval equals the area of one complete dose curve (the part of its tail falling into later intervals is exactly compensated by the earlier tails entering this one). Absorption speed reshapes the curve but cannot change its area.Passing from finitely many previous doses to the periodic profile needs a justified limit under the integral.
